### Control Flow Analysis and Type Narrowing

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/release-notes/TypeScript 4.8.md

Shows how unknown and generic types are narrowed more effectively in truthy branches and how functions can return NonNullable<T> without assertions.

```typescript
function narrowUnknown(x: unknown) {
    if (x) {
        x; // {}
    }
}

function throwIfNullable<T>(value: T): NonNullable<T> {
    if (value === undefined || value === null) {
        throw Error("Nullable value!");
    }
    return value;
}
```

### Narrowing with Loose Equality `!= null`

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/handbook-v2/Narrowing.md

JavaScript's loose equality check `!= null` is used here to narrow a type by excluding both `null` and `undefined`. This allows for safe arithmetic operations on potentially nullable number properties.

```typescript
interface Container {
  value: number | null | undefined;
}

function multiplyValue(container: Container, factor: number) {
  // Remove both 'null' and 'undefined' from the type.
  if (container.value != null) {
    console.log(container.value);
    //                    ^?

    // Now we can safely multiply 'container.value'.
    container.value *= factor;
  }
}
```

### Optional Chaining: Optional Property Access (TypeScript)

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/release-notes/TypeScript 3.7.md

Demonstrates optional property access using the ?. operator. This allows safely accessing nested properties of an object that might be null or undefined, preventing runtime errors. It's equivalent to a ternary check for nullish values.

```typescript
let x = foo?.bar.baz();
```

```typescript
let x = foo === null || foo === undefined ? undefined : foo.bar.baz();
```

### TypeScript Control Flow Analysis Example

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/release-notes/TypeScript 5.5.md

Demonstrates TypeScript's control flow analysis for tracking variable type changes. It shows how a variable's type is refined within an if statement after a check for undefined.

```typescript
interface Bird {
    commonName: string;
    scientificName: string;
    sing(): void;
}

declare const nationalBirds: Map<string, Bird>;

function makeNationalBirdCall(country: string) {
  const bird = nationalBirds.get(country);
  if (bird) {
    bird.sing();
  } else {
  }
}
```

### Equality narrowing

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/handbook-v2/Narrowing.md

TypeScript narrows types in conditional blocks based on equality checks (`===`, `!==`, `==`, `!=`) and `switch` statements. When two variables are found to be equal, TypeScript infers that their types must also be equal, considering only their common types. This also applies to checks against specific literal values. JavaScript's looser equality checks (`==`, `!=`) are also handled correctly, with `== null` checking for both `null` and `undefined`, and `== undefined` checking for either `null` or `undefined`.
